title: The hypertrophy series: using intensity to assess risk to reward ratios
summary: NH explains how intensity can be used as a tool to judge the injury risk vs hypertrophy reward of each lift. Injuries happen at the transition from negative to positive, so lifts starting with an eccentric (squat, bench, good morning) are riskier at high intensity; he keeps good mornings at 6-12 reps and his own squats at 4+ reps, while pushing heavy deadlifts.

claims.claim: Intensity gauges how much exertion a lift requires, feeds tonnage calculations and long-term progression, and can also help you stay injury-free.
Some lifts respond badly to high intensity for nearly everyone; others are risky for you specifically because of your leverages and injury history.
Natural bodybuilding is long-term, so an injury is a setback: a period where you can't accumulate tonnage and therefore don't grow; avoid it at all costs.
Intensity doesn't exist outside of volume: a set of 12 can be more intense than a set of 3 depending on weight selection.
Injuries almost always happen when reversing the negative into the positive, at the bottom or start of the concentric, almost never during the eccentric or at the top.
Lifts that start with a negative phase, using elastic energy (squat, bench), are the most dangerous at high intensity.
The deadlift from the floor has only a positive phase and is very healthy; people hurt their backs because they use too much weight, poor form and grind reps.
For some lifts, low reps carry risk that outweighs the modest hypertrophy benefit, so going heavy isn't worth it.
Good mornings put immense stress on the lower back, hamstrings and SI joint at the parallel-to-floor reversal, and can't be safely protected with spotter arms.
Keep good mornings in a 6-10 or 8-12 rep range; heavy 5-rep sets or 1RMs are useless and dangerous for hypertrophy.
He never squats below 4 reps because of his knee injury history; at low reps his squat turns into a good morning or his knees cave. He works in a 4-8 range, still at high intensity.
By contrast he pushes the deadlift very hard and does 2-rep maxes, because it works for him.
Injuries are a byproduct of intensity; refusing to train intensely is detrimental, but intensity can be turned into a gauge for staying healthy.
Volume can similarly be used to judge your ability to recover from work.
